prompt: What is meant by unemployment?

options.text: Long unemployment spells with skill deterioration

options.label: D

explanation: Long duration increases the risks of skill deterioration, reduced confidence and persistent lost output. Short transitions or predictable seasonal re-employment are generally less damaging.

prompt: Which statement best explains why the economic cost of 8% unemployment can differ between two countries?

options.label: A
options.text: Unemployment percentages determine every consequence regardless of workforce characteristics.

options.label: B
options.text: Duration, causes and affected workers' productivity can differ.

options.label: C
options.text: Every unemployed worker necessarily loses exactly the same income.

options.label: D
options.text: Benefit systems cannot affect fiscal costs arising from unemployment.

explanation: The same headline rate can conceal different durations and types of unemployment, different lost output per worker and different benefit arrangements. These affect the size of the economic and fiscal costs.
reference: 4.5 Unemployment | 4.5.4 consequences of unemployment | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A country replaces its claimant-count headline with a labour force survey headline. The new measure is higher. Which statement is necessarily correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Actual unemployment rises

options.label: B
options.text: Employment falls by the entire difference between the two reported estimates

options.label: C
options.text: Changing measures does not prove unemployment increased

options.label: D
options.text: The administrative records contain deliberate falsification of recorded benefit claims

explanation: A change of headline measure does not by itself demonstrate a change in underlying unemployment. Claimant counts and household surveys differ in coverage and criteria, and survey estimates also have sampling uncertainty.
reference: 4.5 Unemployment | 4.5.2 measures of unemployment, with reference to possible difficulties in measurement | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: An unemployed worker receives benefits equal to 60% of previous wages. Which consequence of unemployment is still most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Benefits necessarily make income higher than previous earnings.

options.label: B
options.text: Benefits necessarily prevent every loss of productive output.

options.label: C
options.text: Benefits necessarily reduce government expenditure on unemployment.

options.label: D
options.text: Benefits cushion but do not eliminate the income loss.

explanation: Benefits can cushion the income loss but, at 60% of previous wages, do not fully replace earnings. The economy also still forgoes the worker's potential production.
reference: 4.5 Unemployment | 4.5.4 consequences of unemployment | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A recession raises cyclical unemployment. At the same time, some workers leave declining industries and require retraining. Which conclusion is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: All unemployment must be seasonal because two causes are present

options.label: B
options.text: Structural unemployment cannot exist during a recession

options.label: C
options.text: Unemployment may contain both cyclical and structural elements

options.label: D
options.text: Cyclical unemployment always disappears immediately when workers retrain

explanation: A recession can create demand-deficient unemployment, while longer-lasting industry and skills mismatch can create structural unemployment at the same time.

prompt: Which result would most strongly suggest that unemployment is mainly seasonal rather than cyclical?

options.label: A
options.text: Job losses follow falling aggregate demand across the economy

options.label: B
options.text: Permanent job losses follow closures in declining industries

options.label: C
options.text: Machines replace workers

options.label: D
options.text: Job losses recur at predictable times of year

explanation: A recurring calendar pattern points to seasonal labour demand. Cyclical unemployment instead follows broad changes in aggregate demand and the business cycle.
